title: The highest person
hookLine: beyond what changes and what lasts: why Krishna is called Purushottama
carry: god is beyond both what changes and what lasts
last: TEJAS — THE LIGHT SEATED IN EVERY HEART.

cards: Krishna and Arjuna are still in the chariot, the two armies waiting. Krishna has just said his light is in the sun and in every heart. Now he goes further.
Look at a wave. It rises, curls, crashes, and it's gone. The ocean under it doesn't crash; it was there before this wave and will be there after.

The wave that passes, the water that stays. In five short verses, Krishna names those two, and then a third, beyond both. And he ends the chapter with a claim: know this, and you've done what you came to do.

teach.b: Verse sixteen. There are two persons in this world, the perishable and the imperishable. Kshara, the perishable, is all beings: every body, every life that begins and ends.
Akshara, the imperishable, is called kutastha, the one that stands firm, unchanging.
Verse seventeen: but the highest person is another, called the supreme self, the undying Lord who enters the three worlds and holds them up.

Verse eighteen: because I am beyond the perishable, and higher even than the imperishable, I am known in the world and in the Veda as Purushottama, the highest person. Purushottama is still a name for Krishna and Vishnu.
Here the schools read carefully and differently. For Ramanuja and his school, the three are real and distinct: changing beings, unchanging souls, and the Lord beyond and within both.
For Advaita teachers, the highest person is the one reality, and the other two are how it appears to us.

Verse nineteen: whoever, free of confusion, knows me as the highest person, knows everything, and worships me with their whole being. Verse twenty ends the chapter: this is the most secret teaching, Arjuna.

teach.h: KNOW THIS, AND YOU'VE DONE IT.
teach.b: Knowing this, a person becomes wise, and has done all there is to do. Here is the teaching, plainly: for Hindus, God isn't one more thing in the world, and isn't only the quiet self inside you.

teach.h: THE TWO AND THE ONE BEYOND.
teach.b: God holds both, and is beyond both. So when a Hindu bows to Krishna, they turn toward what holds everything that changes and everything that lasts.

how: Purushottama, the highest person, is a name of Krishna and Vishnu; some Hindus memorize Gita chapter fifteen, which names Purushottama near its close, and recite it whole.

o: a small household god who guards the front door
the first man, the cosmic ancestor of all people
the highest person, beyond what perishes and what lasts

games.q: the two and the one — tap the pairs.

s: Gita 15 names only two persons: the perishable and the imperishable
verse 17: the highest person is another, beyond both.
beyond the perishable, higher even than the imperishable.
every school reads the three the same way
Ramanuja's school reads three real, distinct realities; Advaita reads one reality appearing as the others.

games.q: chapter fifteen ends. what does Krishna say happens to the one who knows this teaching?
o: they must still study all the Vedas.
they become wise and have done all there is to do.
games.why: verse 20: knowing this, a person becomes wise, and has done what is to be done.

practice: Notice what's changing: the breath, sounds arriving and leaving, thoughts passing; that's the perishable. Then notice what hasn't changed since you sat down, the plain fact of being aware, which is closer to the unchanging.
Without trying to picture anything, rest your attention on whatever holds both; you don't have to name it, just let the sitting be wide enough to include it.

wordCard.voice: Purushottama, the highest person. Gita fifteen: the perishable and the imperishable, and beyond both, Purushottama, higher even than the imperishable.

orig.note: Sanskrit: purushottama, purusha (person) + uttama (highest): the highest person, Gita 15.18.

carryVoice: Your line: god is beyond both what changes and what lasts. The wave, the water, and the one beyond both. That's two hundred twelve.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 15.16–15.17 (kshara, akshara, the supreme self)
